header.title: Procli Constantinopolitani Ad Armenios De Fide Epistola [Interprete Dionysio]: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Dionysius Exiguus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's stoa0108f.stoa011.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0108f.stoa011.opp-l: The text has many scanning errors, silently corrected where the sense is clear (e.g. 'sine retlore' = sine rectore, 'Deus forma canens' = forma carens, 'te: it' = fecit, 'ptrus' = purus, 'impossibilis' = impassibilis). Doubtful places: 'rogati throno' read as Deitatis throno; 'sub aspectu pene quae praestolantur adducens adversa. De quibus...' is obscure, rendered tentatively. 'etsi substantia praeferat ... non erit receptibilis innomitus praedicationis respondit' is corrupt; rendered on the assumption of '[angelica] substantia proferat ... in novitate praedicationis'. 'ut quod erat optimum Da lateret' read as 'non lateret'. 'ex terris paradisi' possibly for 'ex deliciis paradisi'. 'nobis volentibus' could be 'nolentibus' (unwilling). 'dialogis' read as diabolus. 'scripta praevaricatio retorperet' read as 'the written [law] lay numb through transgression'. 'ex eo quod existeret' read as 'quod non existeret'. 'illac quAlitatem' read as 'illic dualitatem'. 'in throno superfluum' possibly for 'in Trinitate'. The syllogism 'Quod si Trinitas et Deus Verbum Trinitate conspicitur' supplemented as 'Trinitas [impassibilis] et Deus Verbum [in] Trinitate'. 'quarum interitus erat supremo munitio' and 'rationale corpus' (perhaps genus) are uncertain.

Several scripture references in the edition are wrong: 'Bar. III' is Baruch 3:38; 'Coloss. VIII' is 1 Corinthians 8:6; 'Act. XVII' is Acts 17:31 (given here oddly as Paul's). 'nisi tamen modo Deus v' is corrupt; rendered as 'while nonetheless remaining God' (reading nihilominus manens Deus). 'qUID' read as quae, 'Itilium' as Filium, 'intratam' as ingratam. The sentence 'quando in unam separatam rediere concordiam, et qui univit in duo ... derivatur' is garbled; the rendering is conjectural. In the date, 'v' is taken as XV (Theodosius II's fifteenth consulship, with Valentinian III's fourth, AD 435).

nodes.text: THE LETTER OF PROCLUS OF CONSTANTINOPLE TO THE ARMENIANS ON THE FAITH,
IN THE TRANSLATION OF DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS.
To the most God-loving and venerable bishops and presbyters and archimandrites of the holy orthodox Church throughout all Armenia, Proclus [sends] greeting in the Lord.

Not a little, brothers, has the report of the new tares of error, which the most cunning enemy of our common nature has lately sown in your region, troubled our mind and wounded [it] with the heaviest grief. For a sad report usually wounds unbearably a soul that has not been trained in reflections of this kind. And it hurls its darts the more destructively, fixing them deep, because the danger does not seek the body but strives to overthrow the condition of the mind, spreading the opinion that the venerable garment of the faith has either been torn, lamentably, or stolen away altogether. Every virtue, indeed, is judged worth seeking by those whose reason is not darkened by material things, and every wickedness is rightly judged by right-thinking people as to be fled, since it stands directly opposed to being, itself existing beyond doubt contrary to nature. For as what is most useful must of necessity be guarded, so what is not expedient but is proved hostile must either be driven off when it is present, or carefully guarded against if it is feared that it may come. Virtue, then, has very many forms. This [virtue] has been variously defined, whether by the gentiles, whom error stifles and whose light of discernment ignorance of the Godhead darkens, or by Christians, who, having the eyes of the mind enlightened by right faith, behold the sun of justice more clearly through confession. For the former, wandering in their own counsels as in darkness, and having a sense that rushes headlong without a guide, rely on uncertain thoughts, examining in what they decide nothing but the fluid and unstable nature of visible things, and having the gaze of true contemplation either entangled in temporal causes or blinded by errors. For they say that there are four forms of virtue, that is, justice, prudence, fortitude, temperance; and these, though they are good, nevertheless creep on the ground and are cast down towards earthly things, since they are shown to be lower than the heavenly summit. For they called fortitude the struggle against the flesh; temperance, that which wins victory by subjugating the passions; prudence, that which maintains desirable institutions in civil life; justice, the best fair apportionment. And so, as they supposed, they sanctioned by law an order of life, restraining unmeasured and unlawful appetite by definitions of this kind. But what is lofty and higher than the present life they could neither think nor express; rather, relying on a foolish and darkened heart, they strove, as far as in them lay, to enclose virtue within visible things alone, attributing to it nothing exceptional and worthy of a heavenly dwelling. But those who have the eyes of the heart enlightened through faith, whose leader and teacher is the most blessed Paul, define virtue as that which, always raising us towards God, governs us in good order on earth. This Apostle, then, venerable in all things, enumerates many forms of virtue, but commends above all faith, hope, charity. Of these, faith bestows on human beings goods that are beyond the merit of nature, joining to the invisible [beings] those who still carry about garments liable to many passions. For the way of life of the angels and the other incorporeal powers, whose nature they do not know by reason of the loftiness of [their] state, faith assigns to human beings who walk on the ground and roll in the dust, presenting us to the throne of the Godhead, which is invisible and lacks all form, and imparting a sure illumination of the uncreated nature that remains forever without beginning. It also, scattering material sense by its brightness and overcoming the thick and cloudy gaze of our mind, [enables us] to see clearly those things which can then be seen in part when they are reckoned invisible, and grasped when they are believed to be inaccessible. Hope, however, not deigning, as is said, to cling to dreams, but firmly holding what is believed, already prepares for itself the future in the present, and, to shut out doubt, embraces in thought what is not present as if it were present, bringing what is awaited almost within sight, [despite] adversities. Overstepping the obstacles these present, hope all but joins what is desired to visible things, entirely surpassing the fleeting emptiness of time by love of the things to come. Charity, indeed, is the summit and head of our holy religion. For through it God, though he was continually present on earth, deigned to come to us through the flesh. Both, then, rightly agree with each other: for faith is the mirror of charity, and charity is shown to be the foundation of faith. We believe that God the Word became incarnate impassibly; and we believe it piously, for this faith is recognised as the foundation of our salvation. Therefore we love him who for our sake took the form of a servant, who neither underwent any change of his nature, nor was any increase added to the Trinity. So every Christian who is not rich in faith, hope, charity is not what he is called; but even if he seems to chastise his poor body and to be free from the passions of the soul, advancing in moral virtue only, he by no means attains the crown of victory, since he has not always stretched out towards that knowledge of the Godhead which grants crowns to those who struggle bravely through virtue. And therefore let faith, which (as I said before) is the head of all goods, be kept intact, displaying nothing discordant [with it] by human inventions, troubled by no profane novelties of words; [faith] which, remaining within the evangelical and apostolic bounds, is to be violated by no one's obstinate fury. For through it we have been saved, and to it we subscribed with our tongue in baptism. For the height of the faith lays low all the audacity and rashness of one who rises up [against it], and not human [audacity] only, but also that of those who are exalted by an incorporeal nature, as blessed Paul says (Gal. 1): Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you anything besides what you have received, let him be anathema. For an angel is commanded to minister, not to compose doctrine. And it is very dangerous for each one not to remain in those [ranks] to which they have been appointed, but to wish to seek beyond measure what has by no means been granted to [their] nature. And therefore even if [an angelic] substance should put forward something that seems worthy of belief, [any] novelty of preaching will not be acceptable. What we have received, then, let us keep with sleepless [care], continually raising the eyes of the mind to the treasure of the faith. And what have we received from the Scriptures, except that God founded the world by his word, and brought forth from nothing the creation which did not exist? And because he honoured the rational animal with a natural law, a command was given to him, so that what was best should not be hidden from his choice, but that he should turn from harmful things by a better purpose. And [we have received] that he, sliding by his own free will into worse things, was cast out of the land of paradise through disobedience; that, finally, through fathers, patriarchs, law, judges and prophets, he who formed nature instructed it to beware of sins and to take care to do what is right; yet so that sins gained dominion even over us, as we willed, and because of them the devil raged to the destruction of nature: since the natural law was growing old and soiled, and the written [law] lay numb through transgression; and the prophets, being men, admonished what ought to be done, but could not deliver from the destruction that threatened; [then] God, lacking form, uncircumscribed without beginning, and the almighty Word, coming in the flesh (for he can do what he wills), took the form of a servant, being made flesh, born of the Virgin, wishing to show everywhere that he deigned to become man in truth. For beginnings, conditions and passions necessarily follow upon a bodily nature. For the evangelist does not say (John 1) that God entered into a perfect man, but that he became flesh, touching the very first beginnings of our nature. For as a man born naturally does not at once come forth perfect in activity, but first, from the very depositing of the seed, flesh is drawn forth, then in the course of time it takes on the power that comprises the completion of the senses and activities; so God the Word, touching the very beginnings and root of human formation, first became flesh, not changed, God forbid, into flesh. For the Godhead remained above all change, because change is a passion of a fluid nature; but it is proper to that perennial and eternal being, which is always thus, to persist unchangeable. Using, then, both expressions of divine Scripture, we say both that he became flesh and that he took the form of a servant. From both, when piously understood, seeds of salvation arise for us: for by [saying] that the Word became flesh, the evangelist declares the indivisibility of the supreme union itself. For as a unity cannot be split into two unities (otherwise, divided into them, it will no longer be a unity but a duality), so what is one according to the supreme union can in no way, by any reasoning, be divided into two. And by [saying] that he took the form of a servant, the unchangeability of the divine nature is indicated: for everything that comes to be either was made from what did not exist, like the heaven which did not exist before; or from what is, it is changed into something else, like the streams of the river Nile changed into blood. But both ways are shown to be unfitting for the divine substance: for he did not come forth from any existing things, remaining always without beginning; nor was God the Word changed from any matter, persisting in his unchangeability. Therefore by these [expressions] divine Scripture testifies both to the unchangeability of the Godhead and to the indivisibility of the mystery, showing what came to be and indicating what he took: so that by the first it commends the singleness of the nature of the person of both, and by the other proclaims the unchangeability of the divine substance. God the Word, then, became perfect man, the nature of the Godhead not being changed, a miracle bearing witness which exceeds the understanding of our mind: this very thing we grasp by faith, we do not gather it by inquiry. And having become man, kin [to us] according to the flesh, he bestowed salvation on the race through likeness of passions, paying the debt of sin, while, having undergone what belongs to man, he dies for all, and destroying him who had the dominion of death, that is, the devil, as the most just God; he also made possible what was impossible for the law, by fulfilling all justice, and restored to our substance its original nobility and glory; by becoming man he honoured him whom he himself had formed from the earth. There is, then, one Son, one Lord: for we confess a Trinity of one essence, by no means admitting a fourth person into the Trinity. But, as we have said, there is one Son, born without beginning from the Father, through whom we believe the ages were made: a branch coeternal with the root, arisen from the Father in an ineffable manner, a word of the mind proceeding inseparably and remaining within. For though he was seen on earth, he was not divided from the one who begot him: he willed to save the one he had made, nay rather he saved [him], graciously dwelling in the womb, the common door of nature, which he both sanctified by his presence and sealed by his birth, showing that the birth, which is beyond nature, was made incomprehensibly man. Christ, then, is not one and God the Word another, God forbid; for the divine nature does not know two sons: one begot one only-begotten; for where there is no union of begetters, there you will not be able to find a duality of those born. In the name of Jesus Christ every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth (Phil. 2). If Christ is another besides God, it must be that Christ is a mere man; and how do heavenly beings worship him beyond the merit of [his] nature, and bend the knee to one who is lesser? How, too, do we heed the prophetic oracles proclaiming that our God was seen on earth and lived among men (Baruch 3)? For by 'vision' the prophet means the manifestation that took place in the flesh, and by 'living among' [the time] in which he dwelt for a season with men, whose ungrudging goodness declared the coming of his loving-kindness: for as almighty, he both remained what he was for his own sake, and became what he willed for our sake. But if perhaps the rudiments of infancy ever give cause for scandal, and the lying in the manger, and the growth in time according to the flesh, and also that he slept in the boat, that he was wearied from the journey, that he hungered after fasting, and all those things which befell him who truly became man: let those who find fault with these things know that they deny the human nature in Christ; and denying the nature, they by no means believe the dispensation; and not believing the dispensation, they will suffer the loss of salvation. And if, since the foundation of the world, by which it is agreed that man was cast into this life, anyone has entered by any other way than this way of the flesh, let the contentious show it, and then at last let them weave their ravings. But if these are the beginnings of common nature, and God the Word truly became man, why do they, confessing the nature, find fault with the passion? Let them choose, then, one of two things: either, ashamed of the insults, let them abjure the nature and, afflicted with the diseases of the Manichees, be counted among the impious; or, if they accept the gain that comes from the incarnation, confessing the substance, let them not be ashamed of the passions that follow upon the substance. I wonder too at the madness of those who walk new paths of deception: for I, acknowledging piously one Son, as I have been taught, confess him to be the substance of God the Word incarnate; and since he who bore the passions and worked the miracles is one, on what reasoning do they keep silent about the more divine things and disparage the humbler? For to produce faith, the Word, remaining what he was, became flesh (John 1), that is, an infant and a perfect man, so great a mystery being violated by no change; the same one performed the miracles and endured the injuries, by the signs indicating that he remained what he was, and by the passions showing that he had become what he had formed. We proclaim, then, one and the same Son, both coeternal with the Father and incarnate in the last times, introducing absolutely nothing spurious into the divine nature: for there can be nothing superfluous in the throne. But perhaps they will put to me that [argument] often spread abroad, weaving syllogisms weaker than a spider's web: If the Trinity is of one essence, surely the Trinity remains impassible. But if the Trinity [is impassible] and God the Word is seen in the Trinity, he remains impassible, and God the Word is shown to be impassible. But if God the Word is impassible, the one who was crucified will be found to be another besides the impassible God the Word. Truly those who bring forward these things weave spiders' webs; those who ponder most foolish propositions write on water; who, though they called themselves wise, became fools, and their foolish heart was darkened (Rom. 1): for a bleary eye does not receive the sun's rays cleanly, and a weak mind cannot gaze on the height of the faith. What, then, do we say to these things? That according to the account of the Godhead the holy Trinity is both of one essence and remains impassible. For when we say that the Son suffered, we do not hold that he suffered in respect of the Godhead, since the divine nature admits no passion whatever; but confessing God the Word, one of the Trinity, incarnate, we give matter for understanding to those who faithfully inquire why he deigned to become incarnate. For since God the Word had resolved to destroy the passions, of which death was held to be the end, and the inviolable nature could not undergo passion (because every passion is shown to bring struggle to composite things, but in a spiritual and single substance there is no composition, nor did passion reach where there was no composition), wishing, as I said before, to destroy the passions which had oppressed the rational body, whose destruction was the supreme safeguard (as God the Word knew), he becomes incarnate from the Virgin, and is found in appearance as a man: since he willed to empty himself in this way, taking in a certain manner the form of a servant (Philippians 2), yet admitting no circumscription of his Godhead, through which he also conferred salvation on the whole human race, exterminating the passions by his flesh while keeping his own Godhead impassible. Therefore Gabriel, intimating the authority and power of the one being born, said to Mary: He will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1). But a people cannot belong to a man, but to God; nor did he who entered this life together with corruption, not having a blameless beginning of birth, rescue the world from iniquities. But of necessity [it was] God and man together, not divided into two but remaining one, showing himself man by being born of a woman, but plainly intimating [himself] God by [being born] without a husband and keeping his mother untouched, [who] saved his people. Who? Jesus Christ, who came upon the earth and dwelt among men (Baruch 3). But if Christ is a mere man, and is not himself God the Word, how did he create all things in the beginning, when then, as the impious assert, he did not exist? For since man is the last among creatures, if Christ is a mere man, it is clear that he could by no means have created the things that were before him, having been made afterwards. And how did Paul say, One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom [are] all things? But if all things were made through Christ, it is manifest that Christ is God the Word, as the evangelist testifies: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; this was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him (John 1). And Paul too, interpreting this, says: One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom [are] all things (1 Corinthians 8). Therefore it is said that Christ is God the Word. But if they bring forward those sayings set out in the divine writings in which Christ is called a man, as Peter says: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you (Acts 2); and as Paul likewise testifies: By the man in whom he has determined, offering faith to all (Acts 17); and as the Lord himself cries out about himself: Why do you seek to kill me, a man (John 8)? let them know that through carelessness they are deprived of the understanding of holy Scripture, or certainly through malice they abandon it, because they wish to twist what has been well written to their own perversity. For Christ is indeed called man in truth, but he became this, which he was not before, while nonetheless remaining God; for as he is God uncreated, so the same one is perfect man, admitting no suspicion whatever of mere appearance. And just as he is consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead, so the same is shown to be like the holy Virgin according to the flesh, the truth of the mystery shining out everywhere and all falsehood entirely removed. But if the virgin did not bear God, neither was the untouched one regarded as a great miracle; for many other women too have brought forth righteous men into the world. For the prophetic tongues, foretelling the ineffability of this mystery, said: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a Son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel; which Gabriel interpreted, saying, God with us (Isaiah 7; Matthew 1; Luke 1). Why, on account of the lowliness of the one being born, do they diminish the glory of the one giving birth? But perhaps they object this, saying: Everything that is born is shown to be like the one who begets it. If therefore it is a man whom she bore, of necessity the one born of her is a man. You put this forward as if by a plausible argument. But one giving birth brings forth one equal to herself in all things when the birth also happens according to nature. But the beginning of natural childbearing is corruption, because intercourse also precedes it. But when there is not even a suspicion of this injury, it is clear that the miracle is above human understanding; where the birth is above nature, there the one born is God. We confess, therefore, that he both made the world from nothing and gave the law, and also inspired the prophets, and was incarnate in the last times, and also sent the apostles for the salvation of the nations and peoples. Let us therefore flee the counsels of seduction, I mean the streams of the heretics, pernicious contagions hostile to God: the madness of Arius, who divides the inseparable Trinity in substances; the audacity of Eunomius, who shuts the incomprehensible nature within the knowledge of humanity; the rage of Mani, who separates from the essence of the Godhead the Holy Spirit, who proceeds inseparably. And also this most recent and new blasphemy, which is known to surpass the impiety of the Jews in many ways. For they, denying the Son, strive to tear the branch from the root; but these, introducing another beside him who is, endeavour to defame the inviolable substance as though [divided] into a manifold offspring. Let us say, then, with Paul (Ephesians 2): Christ is our peace, who made both one. For he re-formed Jew and Gentile through baptism into a new man, joining by power those whom their way of life kept apart. Therefore let the inventors of the new impiety tremble at the condemnation that threatens them, since [those who were] separated have returned into one concord, and he who united is, as far as they are concerned, divided into two. But leaving aside now the length of discourse, I shall come to a summary of right doctrine. If anyone wishes to know truly how the same one is one, and is not only the Son of Abraham, remaining [God], and in the last times advancing in wisdom and age according to the flesh (for his Godhead always possesses what is perfect), let him ask Paul, and he will at once thunder out the mystery of godliness, showing that, though sprung from the Jews according to the flesh, he exists as eternal God. For speaking of the Hebrews and praising the rebellious and ungrateful nation, namely on account of the root, Abraham, and on account of the seed, Christ, he declares thus: To whom, he says (Romans 9), belongs the adoption of sons. For he cries in the prophets: Israel is my firstborn son; and the glory. For divine miracles conferred infinite glory on those who were then approved in their conduct; and the covenants, through which the multiplication of seed was promised to Abraham; and the giving of the law, which was written on the mountain by the finger of God; and the service by which they served in divine worship; and the promises, by which either the land of Palestine or indeed the blessing in the seed of Abraham was conferred on all nations; whose are the fathers, who are shown to have risen in this night of ignorance like lamps of faith, and from whom [is] Christ. Nor did the most blessed Paul stop at these words. For the essence of the Word, existing without beginning, does not date from the time of the birth from Mary. But he at once added, according to the flesh, so as to signify the manifestation that took place in the flesh, not that divine and eternal birth. Who, then, would this Christ be, who was born of the Virgin, whom a cave received as a thing of no value, who lay in a manger, who grew with time according to the flesh, and who, descending to the lower parts of the earth, endured by a wonderful condescension all things that belong to the flesh, to give assurance that he truly became man, and that he is none other than the one who descended, but the same who descended is he who ascended; for he did not first ascend, but descended, as one who is God not by promotion, but who for the mercy we needed condescendingly became man? Who he is, let him not ask of me or of anyone else, but of the Apostle, who says the Son [was made known] by the Father's revelation, when he says (Galatians 1): But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother's womb and called [me] by his grace, to reveal his Son in me. For who this is, he will truly teach, crying out (Romans 9): From whom [is] Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for ever. These words of Paul, what room for slanderous subterfuge do they allow to those who love perverse things? For he said Christ, to show that God truly became man; he said [he was] from the Jews according to the flesh, to intimate that he does not exist only from the time he was incarnate; he said he who is, to declare him without beginning; he said over all, to proclaim him Lord of all creation; he said Lord, lest, led astray by [his] passions and appearance, we should dare to deny his inviolable substance; he said blessed, that we should adore him humbly as almighty, and not assail him with slanders as a fellow servant; he said for ever, to show that he who created us by a word, in accordance with his divinity, should be celebrated by us with unceasing honour. Having therefore Christ both existing, and God, and blessed for ever, let us venerate him as Lord, saying to the advocates of foreign doctrines: If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his (Romans 8); but we have the mind of Christ. Therefore we also await the coming of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, who will render the crown of glory to those who live piously, but to those who provoke him he will repay what their audacity deserves. These things we send to your charity in reply to your petitions, which you took care to dispatch to us, declaring that certain pestilent men, uttering monstrous words, had burst into your province, wishing by certain writings and the oppositions of knowledge falsely so called to pervert the simple and unpainted beauty and steadfastness of the right faith. But I admonish you again with the words of blessed Paul (Colossians 2:8): See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men who take counsel over vain things, and not according to Christ. For no one can lay another foundation of the holy faith than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. Stand therefore in one spirit, of one mind, labouring together for the faith of the Gospel, and in nothing be frightened by the adversaries (Philippians 1), keeping the traditions you have received, whether from the holy and most blessed Fathers who are known to have promulgated the faith at Nicaea, or from the holy and venerable Basil, Gregory, and the others who held the same views, whose names are written in the book of life. I and those who are with me greet very warmly all the brotherhood that is with you in Christ.
[These words are lacking in the Greek.] Given at Constantinople, in the consulship of the most pious Theodosius Augustus for the [fifteenth] time and Valentinian for the fourth.
